entries.title: Running Out of Nails to Bite
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What we learned from last night’s primaries. The Gang of Eight heard about the Air Force One switcheroo the same way you did. Pressuring DHS over Corey Lewandowski. The VA is bringing down its claims backlog, but there’s a catch. And: From Ecuador, what happened after a man got deported.





THE LATEST

There are clear takeaways from last night, the last major primary night before the November midterms. One: Democratic primary voters are increasingly uninterested in older candidates — Rep. John Larson (D-Connecticut), 78, was handily defeated by 47-year-old Luke Bronin, the former mayor of Hartford.

Two: Donald Trump’s endorsement has its limits. Sen. Darline Graham is headed to a runoff with Rep. Ralph Norman (R-South Carolina) in the Republican primary for the Senate seat recently held by Graham’s late brother, despite Trump backing her appointment and her election bid. And Mike Lindell lost the Republican gubernatorial primary in Minnesota to Lisa Demuth despite the president’s support.

Three: In general, it remains very difficult to predict just what the heck is going on! Minnesota’s Democratic Senate primary, which was predicted to be very close in the polls, was in fact not at all close — progressive candidate Peggy Flanagan blew out centrist Angie Craig by double digits.

The Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin was another nail-biter in a year full of them. Progressive Francesca Hong did not win in the landslide many predicted. In fact, she lost to establishment-backed David Crowley. This was an outcome exactly zero public polls predicted.

Open tabs: Amanda Janoo wins Vermont’s Democratic governor primary (VTDigger); Hunter Biden Is Now Everywhere. What Does He Want? (WSJ) Inside Trump’s college sports lobbying push (Semafor); Federal Employees Can Use TikTok Again (NOTUS); A rally involving Max Miller was canceled over threats, but local police say they never heard about them (Cleveland.com)





From the White House

Gang of Eight Democrats say they weren’t briefed on Air Force One decoy scheme: “Nope” was all Rep. Jim Himes (D-Connecticut), the top Democrat on the House’s intelligence committee, texted NOTUS’ Kadia Goba when she asked. The office of Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia), Himes’ upper chamber counterpart, also said he never received a briefing. Some Republican members of the Gang of Eight didn’t respond to requests for comment. Senate Republican Leader John Thune declined to comment.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement that he also had not been briefed (he’s a Gang of Eight member, too). “It is unacceptable that Congress was kept in the dark and instead learned about this serious threat through press reports,” Schumer said.

Trump confirmed to reporters last night that he switched planes at the behest of the Secret Service and the military. “I just follow what they like to do,” the president said, NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause reports.

There were a number of stories yesterday on what was normal about the plane swap in Turkey, and on what wasn’t. The latest came from The New York Times: With Trump Secretly Evacuated, Imperiled Air Force One Became a Flying Decoy.

From the Hill


Democrat presses DHS for answers on Corey Lewandowski: Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-New Hampshire) has an open probe into the former top aide to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Lewandowski has come under bipartisan scrutiny for the way his team handled federal contracts worth big money while Noem was in charge. Noem’s replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, and the new guy in charge of contracts at the department, Under Secretary for Management Brian Cavanaugh, have publicly committed to reviewing the Lewandowski era. Last night, Hassan told Cavanaugh in a letter that she wants to see some results from that review by Sept. 1.

THE BIG ONE

What it’s like to be deported: NOTUS’ Jose Pagliery has been communicating for months with a 44-year-old Cuban man named Rogelio Bolufé, who was arrested in Miami last August and shuffled through the detention infrastructure — “Alligator Alcatraz” and many places like it — before being shipped to Guayaquil, Ecuador, in June. Bolufé is one of thousands of people set to be deported to third countries under administration policy.

His is a surreal tale. He alleges the U.S. did not send him with his Cuban passport, and instead gave him false Ecuadorian documents on the tarmac when he arrived. But those were taken by Ecuadorian officials. And so, 30 minutes into his new life, this was his circumstance, as Jose writes it: The U.S. government had ditched Bolufé in a foreign country with no money, no cell phone and no passport. His drab prison uniform, disheveled hair and two-month scraggly beard made him unapproachable.

The place he was sent to is extremely dangerous, and local government help has not been forthcoming. “In reality, I’m quite alone here,” Bolufé said.

The details of how he has put a meager life together are fascinating, but Jose’s in-depth look at inside the deportation system and his reporting on the apparent false promise of welcoming third countries for American deportees is truly remarkable.

The Department of Homeland Security says Bolufé has dual citizenship in Ecuador, which he denies. DHS denied Bolufé’s allegations of mistreatment in federal detention. “Being in detention is a choice,” a department spokesperson said. “The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now.”

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: Inside a D.C. Courthouse Pushed to Its Limit Under Trump, by Jenny Gathright

Sports desk: Venerated D.C.-area sports columnist Thomas Boswell’s NOTUS debut: This Powerhouse Nats Offense Is a Terrible Thing to Waste

ON NOTUS PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: On today’s episode of On NOTUS, Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon) says Congress must act to limit President Trump’s powers. “If we think of the Constitution as a house, we’ve got holes in the roof, we’ve got termites in the walls, we’ve got crumbling foundation, and we better repair it all,” he told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic. Merkley also discussed socialism versus progressivism and his plans if he becomes chair of the Senate Budget Committee.


NEW ON NOTUS

“Egregious” mistakes: Internal Veterans Affairs data obtained by NOTUS’ Eric Katz backs up fears that the department is denying veteran claims to move quickly on them. The result, according to a broad swath of sources Eric talked to, is an increase in errors. Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins has touted his department’s progress in slashing its claims backlog.

“At the end of the day, the number one thing is making the numbers, making the secretary look good, because if you don’t there’s going to be a problem,” one Veterans Benefits Administration employee said. “Everyone is afraid.”

A VA spokesperson said internal metrics show accuracy rates increasing.

entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: an overcrowded D.C. courtroom, JLG’s listening sessions and Thomas Boswell on the Nats.



THE LATEST

If you want to see how President Trump has changed policing and prosecution in this city, the basement of the D.C. Superior Court is a good place to start.

It’s where NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright spent Monday, Aug. 3, watching initial hearings for people who had been locked up over the weekend.

There, in courtroom C-10, was the usual snapshot of societal challenges that bring people in contact with police and jail: violence, addiction, mental illness, poverty. But the cases that day also showcased Trump’s effect on D.C.’s court system.

Last August, he declared a crime emergency in D.C., seized temporary control of the city police department and flooded the streets with federal agents. Jeanine Pirro, whom he appointed the city’s top prosecutor, ordered the lawyers in her office to seek the toughest possible charges for street crime in the nation’s capital.

What happened in the aftermath? More police stops, more felony charges filed in court and more people locked up in the D.C. Jail.

A year later, that heavy policing and prosecution continues — and the records from the Aug. 3 court appearances show it: In those cases where court filings were publicly available, federal officers were present for half of the arrests. A quarter of the charging documents Jenny was able to review specifically stated that officers were patrolling as part of Trump’s “D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force,” the team he created last year to intensify policing in the District.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Capital One Arena renovation rendering (2048x1366, AR: 1.50)
Capital One Arena is getting a new look. New renderings released Tuesday give fans a glimpse at the reimagined stadium’s exterior, food hall and an immersive video wall, Axios D.C. reports. The three-year renovation is set to finish next fall.

Janeese Lewis George wants to hear from you. The winner of June’s Democratic primary will hold listening sessions in each of the city’s eight wards starting in early September. She says the sessions are to “hear what’s working, what needs to change, and what you want your government to do better.”

A corner store on Capitol Hill has been brought back to life — by its neighbors. Mott’s Market just south of Lincoln Park is now officially back in business, after a topsy-turvy sale and renovation that was funded in large part by 100 nearby residents who didn’t want to see the century-old neighborhood staple disappear. City Cast D.C. has the heartwarming story.

Mayor Muriel Bowser praised the Commanders’ choice of contractors to build out the team’s new $3.8 billion stadium, which was announced Tuesday as a joint venture between D.C.’s Clark Construction, Mortenson and Smoot Construction.

“This is the team that will get it done — they have extensive experience in DC and a proven track record with building iconic sports venues,” Bowser said in a statement. “With this decision, we’re one step closer to transforming 180 acres of land on the banks of the Anacostia into a Super Bowl-ready stadium, and then housing, entertainment, park space, and more.”



FROM VIRGINIA

An ICE agent pulled a gun on a Virginia woman as she drove through a Falls Church parking lot on Monday, NBC4 reports. Rep. Don Beyer posted on X that his office will be “demanding answers and consequences.”





FROM MARYLAND

Business owners in Prince George’s County are suing over a $5,000 annual fee assessed on liquor stores, tobacco stores, gun stores and consolidated storage businesses, saying it amounts to a vice tax that the state would need to sign off on, WTOP reports.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND

For the reader: Chang-rae Lee talks “A Tender Age” at Politics and Prose, Thursday.

For the traditionalist: Montgomery County Agricultural Fair in Gaithersburg, Friday to Aug. 22.

For the music lover: “American Mosaic” played by the National Symphony Orchestra at Wolf Trap, Saturday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Thomas Boswell is back. After five decades covering D.C. sports at The Washington Post, the award-winning columnist makes his NOTUS debut this morning with some thoughts on the Nats and their owners. A preview:

The Lerners should have ponied up for a [bullpen] out of common decency. When you charge the fifth-highest prices in MLB to attend a game, driven by the second-highest concession costs in the sport, then, no matter the bleak preseason prophecies, you don’t field a roster with No Bullpen At All. Even if you think you’ll go 66-96 again, as Las Vegas predicted, you still owe customers a bullpen that can hold a fat lead with two innings to play. Not turn a 9-1 lead into an 11-10 loss. Unless, of course, you want to drive your fans to drink — with a 16-oz beer for $15.40.  

Read the full column here.

Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that Daronte Jones, the Commanders’ new defensive coordinator, is already making an impact. Throughout camp, defensive players have lauded Jones’ teaching ability and principles. In his press conference Tuesday, Jones said he wants to build a unit that plays with confidence and calm.

“[The offense] is trying to get the defense to get rattled, get nervous,” Jones said. “But if we just understand that motion causes emotion and our best ability is to stay ahead of a call, that allows us to calm things down and be slower in our processing.”

What to Watch Today

entries.title: The VA’s Race to Shrink Its Backlog Is Leading to ‘Egregious’ Mistakes
entries.summary: A trail of denials, inaccurate decisions and prolonged appeals processes have left veterans without benefits.
entries.content:
Paul Rushing had a stroke at age 54 and a pulmonary embolism without any of the typical underlying issues. He has a hard time walking 100 yards without having to rest.

In Rushing’s estimation, the issues stem back to his time in the Army when he was exposed to toxic chemicals while serving at Fort Polk in Louisiana, later found to have unsafe levels of “forever chemicals” in its groundwater.

Earlier this year, the Department of Veterans Affairs denied Rushing’s claim. The department’s justification confounded him; it said a doctor had found that his illness was not connected to his service, something his doctor had never even evaluated. The denial letter mentioned medical issues entirely unrelated to his situation.

“Copy-paste errors” from a response to another veteran, Rushing concluded.

The Trump administration has committed to “faster decisions, better service and more benefits for the men and women who have worn the uniform,” as Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins said in July. Its efforts have ushered in remarkable progress: the backlog of claims — defined by cases that have languished for at least 125 days — now sits at around 70,000, down from more than 400,000 in March 2024.

Those results, however, have come at a cost, VA employees, attorneys, advocates and veterans themselves said: The Trump administration keeps getting things wrong.

“We’re getting more decisions but they’re not good decisions,” said Wesley McCauley, an accredited agent who assists veterans in navigating their claims as CEO of United Veteran’s Disability, adding that the mistakes increasingly do not involve complex legal matters. “These are just very clear errors that just should not be missed with just a little bit of review.”

In its efforts to cut through the backlog, the administration’s mistakes have instead drawn out cases in appeals’ processes.

The number of pending “higher-level reviews,” an intermediary step for veterans seeking a second review of their claim before going to the Board of Veterans’ Appeals, has seen a 100% spike since Trump took office.

An appeals board employee, one of roughly 1,000 attorneys on the panel that veterans can turn to if their claims are denied, said their agency was receiving more cases from the regional offices with “very basic errors,” including “egregious” mistakes that “would have been caught in times past.”

“The errors that we’re seeing have just been exploding in the last year and a half,” said Derek Debus, who leads the Stone Rose law firm’s military and veterans practice. His office is emailing adjudicators 10-15 times per week because they missed something on a claim.

Rushing currently has multiple higher-level reviews pending. In July, he sent a supplemental doctor’s note — from a VA physician — linking additional health issues to his service.

The VA responded in just days, again denying the claim. The adjudicator failed to assess the new evidence, according to documents reviewed by NOTUS.

The VA stipend would “allow me to focus on my health and not be out chasing dollars every day,” Rushing said. “It wouldn’t replace my income but it would make life easier.” In the meantime, Rushing is still working every day.

***

Earlier this year, the Veterans Benefits Administration told staff if the agency met its lofty “Freedom 250” goals for backlog reduction, employees would receive an extra day off and 10 days of telework. That was the carrot.

There was also a stick.

Collins has made it harder for staff to meet production and availability targets. He unilaterally terminated the VA’s union agreements last year, and while the matter remains subject to litigation, it has, in the meantime, allowed him to impose new conditions on employees without negotiation. Shortly after terminating the union contracts, the VA increased the quota of cases for appeal board attorneys. Collins also reinstated mandatory overtime and increased automation.

The work environment has driven burnout and mistakes, employees said. They are facing extraordinary pressure from their supervisors and VA headquarters to produce at all costs, likening VA disability claims to widgets that must be processed.

“At the end of the day, the number one thing is making the numbers, making the secretary look good, because if you don’t there’s going to be a problem,” one Veterans Benefits Administration employee said. “Everyone is afraid.”

Any staffer who misses their production or availability targets — employees must be actively working on cases 80% of the work hours in a given year — is subject to a performance improvement plan that can lead to termination. Employees lamented that they no longer get a reprieve from management’s demands when they are having IT issues, meet with a supervisor, sit in trainings or even when the VA’s systems are down. Employees who take 12 weeks that the government allows for paid parental leave, for example, would not hit the 80% annual availability requirement.

“There has been a bigger push to get cases out as quickly as possible,” another Veterans Benefits Administration employee said. “The pressure is there to produce, produce, produce.”

Veterans Benefits Administration staff are “rushing through files and making mistakes, and that’s a disservice to the veteran,” one worker said. Given their burdens, said Debus, some staff are “incentivized to say, ‘AI said it’s good, I’ll just click approve.’”

The VA’s approach is self-serving, several employees said: If a veteran appeals a denied claim, it resets the clock for the case back to zero; it makes the backlog look smaller without actually resolving a veteran’s need.

Internal VA data obtained by NOTUS supports fears that the department is just denying claims to move quickly. The VA denied 35% of claims in fiscal year 2024, the last year fully under then-President Joe Biden's watch. That jumped to 38% in fiscal year 2025 and climbed to 39% in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026. The department completed nearly 30,000 more claims in October through December 2025 compared to the same period two years prior, though it granted 9,000 fewer.

Employees are evaluated for how quickly they move cases but face less pressure for accuracy.

“There’s a lot of pressure to get these claims adjudicated quickly, even if it's sloppily done,” the board attorney said. “The problem is it doesn’t really address the root issue of the backlog if you’re just denying claims arbitrarily. We have to remand, and it goes back to the regional office and they have to correct that.”

Some of the cases are so complex they involve thousands of pages, or have festered for so long that they include notes hand written during the Vietnam War. Attorneys with the agency are “absolutely” making more mistakes in the current environment, an employee said, and are remanding cases after they find the first mistake instead of conducting a comprehensive review.

“If there are additional errors, that’s someone else’s problem to address because you need to hit your production goal,” the board attorney said. The quota creates “perverse incentives. Everything is just about the numbers so you have to push the numbers as fast as you can.”

Around 97% of Board of Veterans’ Appeals attorneys said the new quotas “increased the likelihood of factual or legal errors in board decisions,” according to a recent survey of staff commissioned by the American Federation of Government Employees chapter that represents the employees. Ninety-three percent said they no longer had time to conduct a completely fresh review of an appeal.

“Respondents described spending less time reviewing case files, supporting evidence and legal authorities in order to meet the biweekly quota,” according to the survey.

Quinn Slaven, a VA spokesperson, said the administration’s approach has led to its success in lowering the backlog so dramatically. He noted that the VA’s internal metrics show accuracy rates increasing.

“Whereas the Biden administration judged the department’s performance by how many people it employed and how much money it spent, the Trump administration is solely focused on measuring VA’s success by how well it serves veterans,” Slaven said.

As for the promised day off and telework, the Veterans Benefits Administration missed its stated goal of bringing the backlog down to its lowest point ever. While the agency got below 70,000 claims, it fell just short of its 64,000-claim goal.

“They were teasing the extra day off only to say, ‘Oh sorry, you didn’t meet it,’” another Veterans Benefits Administration employee said.

***

The VA saw a rush of new claimants after Biden signed the PACT Act in 2022, a bipartisan law that made millions of veterans newly eligible for benefits for toxic exposures during their service.

In anticipation of a surge in claims, the Veterans Benefits Administration added 7,300 claims processors, a more than 50% increase, under Biden. The case inventory fell nearly in half between its spike in early 2024 and Trump’s inauguration, as new hires got trained up and put on the job. The more recent headway marks a continuation of that trend.

The Veterans Benefits Administration has shed 2,400 claims processors under Trump, though it recently began to reopen hiring for the roles. Overall, the VA’s benefits shop has lost 5,000 employees under the current administration, or 15% of its workforce.

Staffing shortages have only exacerbated pressures, employees said.

The VA is walking a tightrope as it slashes its claims backlog, with congressionally chartered veterans service organizations like Veterans of Foreign Wars warning Congress that the department cannot sacrifice accuracy for speed.

The VA has insisted its accuracy has not waned during its recent push, a claim supported by its public-facing data. Around 83% of claims are error free, an increase from a nadir of around 79% when the backlog hit its recent high point in 2024.

Some outside groups and attorneys have questioned the VA’s methodology, though the department has said it draws from a statistically significant random sample. Scott Hope, the national service director for Disabled American Veterans, said the public has little insight into the internal data that underlies the VA’s public error rates. The group has asked the department’s inspector general to examine that process, he said.

Lisa Van Haeren, director of the VA inspector general’s evaluations and audits office, told NOTUS that the Veterans Benefits Administration is so production oriented that “it’s at the expense of quality.” She noted the agency internally uses a limited checklist to identify errors, whereas the inspector general’s auditors aim to identify any claim decision misaligned with department policy or federal law.

“We find a higher error rate” than the VA does internally, Van Haeren said.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims — a body outside the executive branch where veterans can take their case if they are unsuccessful before the VA’s internal board — saw appeals spike to a record high in fiscal year 2025 as the VA processed more claims. Cases that reach that level have historically maintained a high remand rate, a trend that continued under Trump and Collins. Of the more than 10,000 appeals before the court it received in fiscal year 2025, 9,600 of them contained errors.

“How can you say we’re reversing the backlog if the court is drowning,” said McCauley, the veterans advocate.

One employee, who works on cases involving military sexual trauma, said the work, coupled with the mandatory extra hours and pressure from management, is draining. Some days, the burden becomes personal.

“I don’t feel like I did a good job for these veterans today,” the employee recalled recently telling a family member. “I’m really tired. I feel really guilty about it.”

Like others, the employee said they are driven by the mission to serve veterans and a desire to treat every claim “with the utmost care because they are real people behind the paper.”

“Some days I go, ‘Did I do a good enough job on that person?’” the staffer said, begrudging VA management for the unrelenting intensity the workplace demands have placed on employees. “I want to do a good job for the veteran, but they make it hard.”

entries.content:
I haven’t needed an intro for 57 years, but here goes:

Glad to be back!

Now, where were we?

One of the rarest achievements for any baseball team is to lead MLB in runs scored, home runs and stolen bases in the same season. Only the most powerful, swift and dynamic offenses have done it since the Lively Ball Era began in 1920. 

Until now, that distinction belonged to the ’31 New York Yankees with Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Billy Dickey and the Boys of Summer of the Brooklyn Dodgers with Jackie Robinson, Gil Hodges and Duke Snider who performed the feat in ’52, ’53 and ’55. 

Now, for the first time in more than 70 years, another team leads MLB in all three of those glamour categories.

The Washington Nationals.   

You can now clean up the coffee you just spilled all over yourself.

Last season, the Nats were 24th in homers, 20th in runs and 10th in steals. With 41 games left, the Nats already have 13 more homers (174) than they hit all of last year.

If Washington baseball fans find themselves shaking their heads in delighted disbelief, there’s good reason. Since 1901, in a total of 91 previous MLB seasons for the old Senators of the American League and the new Nats of the National league, Washington has never had a team that led MLB in runs scored. Or homers.

Normally, I’m semi-friendly, but let’s make a brief exception. If the Nats owners had given new team president Paul Toboni an additional $10 million to $15 million in the offseason for his tiny payroll to provide for perhaps the 20th best bullpen in MLB, rather than Washington’s opening day dog mess, the Nats would’ve allowed about 40 fewer runs this season — implying a likely 90-win pace now. Playoffs, why not?

This is 20-20 hindsight. But it's also a case of: Your sins will find you out. The Lerners should have ponied up for a pen out of common decency. When you charge the fifth-highest prices in MLB to attend a game, driven by the second-highest concession costs in the sport (according to my new research assistant, ChatGPT), then, no matter the bleak preseason prophecies, you don’t field a roster with No Bullpen At All. Even if you think you’ll go 66-96 again, as Las Vegas predicted, you still owe customers a bullpen that can hold a fat lead with two innings to play. Not turn a 9-1 lead into an 11-10 loss. Unless, of course, you want to drive your fans to drink — with a 16-oz beer for $15.40.

If the Lerners had been good MLB citizens, then they could still have made their sensible deadline deals of hitters Curtis Mead and Luis García Jr. to add young pitchers. No matter their record at the deadline, the Nats should have made a far harder push to extend All-Star pitcher Foster Griffin. Overpay him? Yeah. After all, they just saved $12 million on the ’26-’27 salaries they don't have to pay García.

Enough with the “if only” regrets. This year just reinforces my Lerner view from last season: Fund it or sell it.

Instead, though, let’s focus on the Nats’ offensive shock waves. This season underlines that former general manager Mike Rizzo and his staff were excellent scouts of talent. Of the Nats’ 171 homers, 144 are by players from that regime.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But it’s also clear that Toboni and a radically transformed organization, including three hitting coaches with three different specialties, are better at modern player development — at least in hitting.

The Nats’ marriage of preexisting talent and improved player development methods is likely to continue showing dramatic results. Player development now includes many new areas, including biomechanics and motion capture to record kinetic chain efficiency in live play, plus mechanical optimization to pinpoint pitching delivery flaws or improve a hitter’s swing path. Every degree of joint flex is debriefed.

The words get fancy. But, for me, one reason the Nats are on pace to score 178 more runs is that, whether they know it or not, they are following Babe Ruth. Asked how he hit, he said, “Pick out a good one and sock it.”

Picking out a good one is incredibly hard. Now, they use terms like “improved pitch recognition” or “controlling the strike zone” or knowing which pitches in which areas the computer says suit your swing the best.

But it’s still just “picking out a good one.” As for “sock it,” the two concepts go together. If the pitch isn’t a good one — for you — how can you belt it off the fence or over it? The Nats are looking for pitches to clobber, not just make contact, or they spit on ’em. That’s why they also lead MLB in extra-base hits, total bases and slugging average.

To make matters better, the Nats position players are the youngest in baseball at 24.9 years of age. As a group, they should ripen.

The Nats don’t figure to get much older any time soon. Just look at Rochester. Their AAA affiliate, the Redwings, are scoring even more runs this season (5.55 per game) than the Nats (5.34), despite home games in a "pitcher's park." And they are doing it almost entirely with talent the Nats already had on hand. For months, Rochester had so many players with gaudy stats they’d have needed 11 positions to use them all at once.

So, it was no surprise that Abimelec Ortiz (74 RBI in 312 at-bats at Rochester) homered in his first MLB at-bat, while Andrew Pinckney waited until his second MLB at-bat to homer.

Right now, slick-glove infielder Trey Lipscomb, who’s become a 20-homer, .858 OPS hitter this year, can’t get out of AAA. Neither can first baseman Yohandy Morales with 23 homers and a .926 OPS. Shortstop Seaver King, the No. 10 overall pick in ’24, has shot up to AAA where his OPS is .800.

Rizzo’s last big pick, No. 1 overall Eli Willits in ’25, has played 88 games at age 18 at A and A+ this year. The switch-hitting shortstop has 87 runs, 81 walks, 47 steals, 13 homers and an .893 OPS. Juan Soto and Bryce Harper are the only two Nats with such stats at age 18 or 19. They were both in MLB to stay at 19.

Helped by Toboni trades to add prospects, the Nats’ farm system was recently ranked the fourth-best in the game. For years, when the Nats were trading prospects to get the final pieces for a postseason run, they ranked low.

As every Washington fan knows, the Nats’ pitching (28th of 30 in runs allowed) is almost as bad as the offense is good. That’s why the Nats, outscored by 212 runs in ’25, have “only” outscored their foes by 28 runs this season.

Just look at -212 to +28 and smile: A 240-run-differential improvement in one season. The Braves have played in several towns since 1876. They’ve only improved their run differential by that much in a season twice, in 1897 and 1991. Yes, you can wait a century to get that much better that fast.

There are still many miles to go. The horrid pen may’ve improved recently — finally. But the larger question is: What about the Whole Darn Pitching Staff? Answer: That's what hitting prospects are for! Mead and García, who was leading MLB in slugging when traded, won’t be the last bat-for-arms deals.

Those, like me, who bristle that ownership didn’t step up a lot to extend Griffin and improve the pitching picture immediately, should probably calm down. (Unclench your teeth, Boz.)

As much as a club ever does in a sport that shifts a team's image like a kaleidoscope, the Nats have time on their side. The Nats didn’t lose anybody of consequence to free agency until CJ Abrams after ’28. They have so many high-pick maybe-elite middle infielders in the system that they’ll probably trade CJ for starting pitching at some point.

The only meaningful free agent who could leave after the ’29 season is pitcher Cade Cavalli, who may be extended by then. That’s it. Otherwise, everybody at Nats Park now, plus everybody in the minors, plus future draft picks and international signings, plus anyone acquired in a trade, plus any free agents that the Lerners — or possibly new, more confident, less frugal owners at some point — sign as free agents will still be under team control in ’30.

Almost everybody needs a lift these days. When the local baseball team is fun to watch, you feel better for three hours a day, 162 times a year and sometimes in October, too. Even on a flawed team, 865 runs, 230 homers and 175 steals is pretty fun.

Maybe, this season, the Nats will be the first team to lead the majors in runs, homers and stolen bases in the same year since 1955. Or maybe not. But these Nats pass the “enjoyment” test.

When waiting for improvement suddenly turns the corner into confidently expecting better days, watching that gradual daily process becomes its own sweet pleasure.

entries.title: Bethlehem Steel Is Lobbying for a Comeback
entries.summary: Domestic steel production is increasing, and a company using the once-storied name is looking for help in Washington.
entries.content:
In 2003, a steel giant finally crumbled.

Once the second-largest steel manufacturer in the United States, Bethlehem Steel had filed for bankruptcy two years earlier. The cause of death was attributed, in part, to cheaper imports that ate into the domestic steel market.

But now, two brothers are resurrecting the Bethlehem Steel name, and they’re turning to K Street’s professional influencers for help.

The new Bethlehem Steel hired two sets of federal lobbyists this spring: a team of lobbyists at K&L Gates that includes former Rep. Michael Doyle (R-Pennsylvania), and another at Steptoe LLP that includes Kevin Garvey, a former senior trade official during President Donald Trump's first term.

Bethlehem Steel’s resurgence comes amid major changes in the domestic steel industry, including the recent merger of U.S. Steel and Nippon Steel and higher tariffs on steel imports that are steering business toward domestic producers.

“There's increasing demand for American-made steel, and then what we saw with Nippon and U.S. Steel is those steelmakers that have a presence in America are much more valuable,” Brandon Farris, an executive vice president at the Steel Manufacturers Association, told NOTUS In a phone interview.

Bethlehem Steel declined interview requests through K&L Gates.
K&LGates (6240x4160, AR: 1.50)“We’re working to revitalize that company and bring it back and to be the sort of tip of the spear of the reinvigoration of American manufacturing,” James Ganley, who “re-founded” Bethlehem Steel with his brother, Micheál Ganely, told the independent media company RocaNews in December. “The rest of American manufacturing is dependent on a company like this being able to come back.”

Government documents give some clues about the new Bethlehem Steel’s emergence.

Bethlehem Steel Corporation was incorporated by A Registered Agent, Inc. in October 2024 in Delaware, according to the company’s certificate of incorporation.

At that point, Trump was still a few weeks away from winning the 2024 election.

But one policy from his first term had already planted seeds for the regrowth of the domestic steel industry, according to Farris.

In 2018, the Trump administration slapped a 25% tariff on imported steel, making it more expensive to import foreign steel and nudging buyers toward domestic steel.

In June 2025, months into his second term, Trump increased steel tariffs to 50%. Steel product imports have since declined from 13.3 million metric tons for the calendar year ending June 2025 to 10.3 million metric tons for the year ending June 2026, according to Census Bureau data.

Meanwhile, domestic steel production was up 5.7% between Jan. 1 and Aug. 8 this year, or nearly 5.1 million metric tons, compared to the same period 2025, according to the most recent data published by the American Iron and Steel Institute.

“We have another 4 million tons that's expected to come online over the next two years,” said Farris, citing data tracked internally by the Steel Manufacturers Association.

Declan Ganley, CEO of Rivada Networks, announced in an X post last February — around two weeks after Trump was sworn in for a second term — that his sons had “secured the name Bethlehem Steel” and “want to make it the Tesla of steel.”

Micheál Ganley, a former nominations counsel for the Senate Judiciary Committee under the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, signed the amended statement of incorporation in November 2025.

Micheál and James Ganley also stood up a branch of the business in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, last October, according to state incorporation records. Micheál is the CEO while James is president, according to their LinkedIn pages.

It’s not whether the company has begun large-scale commercial steel production. Its hired lobbyists have so far sought funding opportunities while connecting with government officials on capacity issues, according to federal lobbying records.

Bethlehem Steel paid K&L Gates $60,000 between April 1 and June 30 to lobby on “funding opportunities and incentives for project” during the second quarter, the records indicate. The lobbyists disclosed lobbying the Senate, Export-Import Bank of the United States, Department of Energy, Office of Management & Budget, U.S. Trade Representative and the Department of Commerce.

Steptoe reported receiving less than $5,000 to lobby the Department of Commerce on ”industrial capacity and procurement issues,” according to the firm’s second quarter filing.

Neither Micheál nor James Ganley responded to a list of questions from NOTUS, including what specific project they were working on or the status of the business.

“Not knowing exactly what Bethlehem's looking for, I can tell you the equipment piece, writing off the equipment, is something that's big for every one of our members making investments,” Farris told NOTUS.

He also said “the credit for building a new manufacturing facility is also something that our members are looking into heavily.”

Bethlehem Steel’s lobbying operation remains relatively modest compared to other steel giants. The top three domestic steel producers last year were Nucor, Cleveland Cliffs and U.S. Steel, according to the International Trade Administration.

Nucor spent $510,000 on federal lobbying during the second quarter of 2026. The company also hired Miller Strategies, run by prominent Republican lobbyist Jeff Miller, in June to lobby on “issues related to steel production.”

Cleveland Cliffs spent $630,000 during the second quarter of 2026 to lobby on a range of issues including “maintenance and strengthening of Section 232 steel and auto/auto parts tariffs,” according to federal lobbying records. Cleveland Cliffs has significantly increased its lobbying spending from $630,000 during the first six months of 2025 to nearly $1.3 million through the same period in 2026.

U.S. Steel spent $270,000 during the second quarter of 2026 to lobby on a range of issues, including “U.S. manufacturing strategy” and national security issues, according to its most recent lobbying disclosure. The steel giant spent $1 million during the same period last year as it pushed the Trump administration to approve its merger with Nippon Steel, which was finalized in June 2025.

entries.title: Mike Lindell Refuses to Concede After Claiming Election Irregularities
entries.summary: The founder of MyPillow saw his dream of becoming governor put to bed Tuesday by Minnesota voters.
entries.content:
Mike Lindell, the quixotic founder of bedding company MyPillow who rose to prominence as a staunch ally of President Donald Trump after vigorously contesting the results of the 2020 presidential election, is now refusing to concede his own race for Minnesota governor.

Lindell questioned multiple projections that forecast Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth advancing to November’s general election. She led Lindell by about 11 percentage points as of Wednesday morning with 99% of votes counted, according to The Associated Press. Demuth accepted her nomination late Tuesday.

As vote-counting showed Demuth’s lead widening throughout Tuesday evening, Lindell told reporters there appeared to be last-minute “mathematical deviations” in the results. He vowed to get answers and said he refused to recognize any calls made by the AP.

“What is the AP to voters? Why would I listen to the AP?” Lindell replied when asked whether he would concede the race after the wire service made its projection, a common practice for candidates in both parties.

“I’m not going to give up this race until the votes are counted,” said Lindell, whose television network was displaying AP-tabulated results on its website. “That’s nonsense.”

The bedding magnate did not respond to a request for comment from NOTUS on Wednesday morning.

Demuth will face Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar in the November general election.

Lindell’s remarks called back to his yearslong obsession with proving that Trump won the 2020 election, which led to a series of embarrassing missteps that propelled the former crack addict and author to the national spotlight. Lindell’s bushy mustache and throaty upper Midwestern drawl made him a subject of countless late-night parodies and internet memes, though Trump never stopped supporting Lindell’s efforts.

The president endorsed Lindell in July, stating, “Nobody has sacrificed more than Mike Lindell in fighting for our country, especially when it comes to Election Integrity.”

Lindell’s refusal to accept Tuesday’s results quickly drew mockery online.

“Many people say Venezuela rigged the election against Mike Lindell because they don’t like his pillows,” Rep. Ted Lieu (D-California) joked on X. “Never seen anything like it.”

Lindell’s circulation of widely debunked claims of voter fraud have resulted in numerous lawsuits and social media bans — issues that loomed over his gubernatorial campaign.

This summer, he confidentially settled a defamation suit from Dominion Voting Systems, now known as Liberty Vote. In a separate case last year, a federal appeals court ruled Lindell did not have to pay a $5 million reward to the winner of a contest he spearheaded, asking challengers to debunk claims of Chinese interference in the 2020 election — a mandate they promptly fulfilled.

Lindell’s campaign for governor was also marred by several new scandals.

He faced scrutiny over whether he met the residency requirements to run for Minnesota governor after reports emerged that he was registered to vote in Texas. He was also sued for allegedly violating campaign finance rules by distributing promotional pillows at a Fourth of July parade. He said the allegations were a “set-up hit job.”

Lindell stepped down from MyPillow this month to focus on the governor’s race.

entries.title: Workers’ Wage Gains Have Been Erased by Inflation
entries.summary: Energy prices have soared this year since the U.S. began its war with Iran.
entries.content:
Workers aren’t reaping the rewards of higher wages, Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Wednesday shows.

Employees saw a 0.1% increase in average hourly earnings in July. Those gains were wiped out by a 0.1% increase in prices between June and July.

The yearly inflation rate punched in at 3.4% in July. The price pressures can primarily be attributed to rising energy prices, which have soared as Iran strangles the world’s supply of oil transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz as leverage in the war with the U.S.

Fuel prices alone surged 39.1% in the previous year, according to the report.

High energy prices have trickled down to other sectors of the economy, including transportation, apparel and food, which hit a 3% annual inflation rate, deepening the United States’ affordability problems ahead of the midterm elections, where cost of living has taken center stage.

Rising housing costs accounted for two-thirds of inflation changes from June to July.

Overall, real average hourly earnings — workers’ average pay adjusted for inflation — declined 0.1% from June to July. Although workers are taking home a larger average paycheck than they did a year ago, they are effectively earning less in purchasing power, according to the report. Workers have slightly less purchasing power than they did when summer began.

Ben Zipperer, senior economist at the left-leaning Economic Policy Institute, said Wednesday’s report was “unambiguously bad news for workers.”

“They’re now taking a pay cut. A frozen job market has weakened their bargaining power and slowed nominal wage growth, and the higher inflation from Trump's Iran war has caused real wages to decline,” Zipperer said in a text to NOTUS.

Workers have for years faced pressure in their pocketbooks from persistent inflation, which was kicked off by the pandemic and, most recently, compounded by the Iran war. The Trump administration’s continuously changing tariff policies are also raising prices for consumers, as businesses pass on high import costs.

Consumers faced limited relief in July.

Energy prices dipped from June to July as the U.S. and Iran briefly recognized a fragile ceasefire agreement in mid-June. It was one of the few categories where prices declined; medical care, airfares and restaurant prices all rose.

Prolonged inflation is proving to be a thorn in the side of monetary policymakers looking to lower inflation to 2% in the long term. The Federal Reserve has punted interest rate changes at five consecutive meetings, in part due to uncertainty created by the conflict in the Middle East.

However, markets are increasingly becoming convinced that an interest rate increase is on the horizon, which would raise borrowing costs for businesses and consumers to slow spending and bring prices back down. The next interest rate decision will be in mid-September.
